title: Self
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The Buddha teaches that our experience is not defined by a permanent, unchanging self, but rather by interconnected aspects of reality such as form, feeling, perception, impulse, and consciousness. By recognizing this, we can unify body and mind, ground ourselves in the present moment, and find liberation from suffering. This understanding allows us to see things as they truly are, without attachment or identification, leading to a sense of freedom and enlightenment.

sentences.text: We were talking yesterday, saying that the Buddha wasn't so much concerned about the truth, or the nature of the universe, or how things came to be.
He was mostly concerned about suffering.
We all know the story about the Buddha having encountered suffering, left home, and gone on his spiritual quest up until that super dramatic moment under the Bodhi tree.
Everybody knows that story.
And every year in Mexico, during our annual Rohatsu sesshin, I gin myself up to tell this story with full elaboration.
We all get really excited about the Buddha's awakening.
Then we end our sesshin with a really colorful and musical, flower-strewn, outrageous ceremony to celebrate our collective enlightenment.
And it is really great.
Some of you have been there, I know.
You can ask Rick and Arhelia, who have been there many times.
They will tell you that it is probably the greatest, most joyful enlightenment ceremony on earth.
It is, I think.
Modestly, I'm saying this.
I don't think you'll find a ceremony like this anywhere on earth.
So yes, the Buddha's awakening is a very dramatic, joyful, wonderful thing, as we read about it in the Sutras.
But the older I get, the more I'm betting that maybe the Buddha's story in actual fact wasn't quite as dramatic as the Sutras would make us believe.
The story in the Sutras is legendary and mythic, and of course we need legendary and mythic stories.
But probably, more realistically, I bet that the Buddha was constantly working on his practice.
Constantly trying to understand more.
Little by little, day by day, understanding more and awakening more and more and more and opening up more and more and more.
Probably he did have one night or more than one night or many nights of transcendent experiences.
But then the next day, breakfast, lunch, dinner, he just went on.
No dinner, but breakfast, lunch, he went on.
Because there's always more.
From the beginning, he was intent on reducing suffering for everyone.
He was really interested in sharing his practice, and he did do that.
He never had a day off for 45 years of just wandering and teaching and sharing his practice until his final Parinirvana.
And I have no doubt that he learned a lot about practice and about his own life through the process of sharing his life with others.
He saw how the practice and the teaching appeared in the lives of others who were different from him, who received it and understood it differently than he had done.

He must have been adjusting all the time and understanding more all the time, little by little, trying to figure out what's the best way to explain things so that people could be guided out of their thicket and could find at least a little bit of happiness, the way he had found happiness for his own life.
So he was all the time thinking about suffering and how suffering comes to be.
What causes suffering?
How could we undo suffering?
In those reflections, he realized that one of the most important acupressure points of suffering is self: our assumptions, our hidden, unexamined views about self.
So a lot of what he talked about was about self.
What is self?
How does it arise?
How does it condition our suffering?
I think the first and most obvious thing that he noticed was that basically human suffering completely depends on self.
If there's no self, there's no suffering, because I suffer, right?
And if I'm not there, then suffering doesn't bother me.
And he saw that the whole formation of suffering has to do with self.
I assume myself automatically, without questioning.
And myself has needs and wants.

Since the very definition of myself is that it is pretty fragile, one little self compared to billions of other selves in the rest of the big world, therefore myself must constantly be on guard and defend and control and make a world that's safe for myself.
Peering out at the world from the little eyes of myself, I see many things that I want and many other things that I really don't want and that I consider an affront and a threat or a dishonor.
If my self's body is hurt or somehow not looking too good, this is a bad thing.
If I don't get enough credit for being an excellent myself, especially stacked up against the other selves out there, this is already a problem for me.
So I am constantly at work, 24 hours a day, even in my dreams, to promote and protect this self.
And this is an exhausting battle doomed to defeat.
I'm not even mentioning sickness, old age and death here.
Even without sickness, old age and death, which are inevitable disasters, we already have every single day a million frustrations and anxieties and even terrors, whether or not we acknowledge them.
And this is to me the most amazing part: in my sincere desire to be the best possible myself, I can even block myself from myself.

I can even alienate myself from myself so that I become an extremely unhappy and lonely self, which will then give me the compulsion to take out my unhappiness on other poor selves that themselves are going through the same thing.
So the Buddha noticed all this with some clarity.
And he said, all right, let's look into this question of the self.
What is it really, and how does it function?
Let us commence to investigate this.
Fortunately, the Buddha came from a culture in which mindfulness and meditation were ordinarily practiced by sages, and he learned these practices from other teachers.
He used these practices to investigate the nature of self.
As we were saying a few days ago, when you practice mindfulness, when you practice concentration and meditation, you create inner space.
You make space inside that wasn't there before so you can move around and you can see more of what's going on.
So the Buddha said, OK, let's see what kinds of experiences we are having all the time, and let's see if in all those experiences we can find a self.
In other words, let's see how accurate to our actual experience is the assumption of self as we understand it and live it.
Is it really a warranted assumption?
Let's look and see.
The Buddha was the first great phenomenologist, who started not with a theory or a belief, but with a faith in looking and seeing on the deepest possible level.
So what is going on?
We're doing this investigation ourselves, right, this week.
What is going on here, actually?
The Buddha notices there's a body, stuff, material stuff.
The Buddha defined matter as that which can be broken or hurt.
That's the very definition of the physical.
He noticed that things that were not material, like thoughts or feelings or memories, cannot be broken or hurt.
They disappear and disappear, but nothing can hurt them.
A thought can hurt you, but nothing can hurt the thought itself.
Matter, on the other hand, can be broken.
That's its nature.
It can be hurt.
It can be molested.
It is subject to brokenness by its nature.
So that's the first thing he noticed: that there is matter, that physical stuff is a basis for everything else that arises.
Then, built on that basis, there is a whole swirl of non-material experience.
There are sensations, which can be bodily sensations or emotional sensations.
There are perceptions, which are experiences like seeing and hearing and so on, which bring a world into view so that now we're living in a world with others.
Based on those sensations and those perceptions, there will be volitions.
There will be desire.
There will be basic attitudes, moods, and so on: a climate, an inner climate that will condition our experience.
In other words, as I'm sure we're all seeing this week, when there's nothing else to do but really look closely, there's really a lot going on there, right?
There's a tremendous amount of stuff going on.
Simply perceiving something, and all the inner stirrings that go with even a simple, ordinary perception.
We like it.
We don't like it.
We find it subtly, somehow, threatening or alluring or satisfying.

We fit it into a whole framework based on innumerable past experiences so that we can define it and place it in a world in which it belongs, that we have made out of our perceptions and our feelings and so on.
Even a simple perception has all this stuff with it.
Every moment of our experience is really complex.
Mostly, of course, we don't notice any of this.
We don't think about it.
We would all go crazy, of course, if we stopped to notice all that's going on every moment.
So we don't. [unclear: "We don't go forth."] But when we do stop to analyze it, it's really impressive how thick our experience is, how much is going on.
In all of this, you don't actually see anything called the self.
It turns out that the self is a kind of extremely crude and ultimately destructive shorthand for organizing all this experience.
The way that the self organizes all this experience and sets us up to receive experience pretty much guarantees that we are going to suffer, even if no disastrous things happen.

So the Buddha tried to make a simple counter-explanation for experience, an explanation that would account for the fullness of experience without resorting to the crude and basically unsuccessful notion of self.

He said experience is organized into five different types: form, which is matter, the body, things of the physical world; sensations or feelings, which are both physical sensations and [unclear: "root"] psychological sensations; perception with the sense organs; impulses or volitions; and consciousness, which is the field of awareness that makes cognition of all the other four kinds of experience possible.
It's like a light that illuminates everything, so everything pops into view instead of just being there in the dark.
We call these five kinds of experience collectively myself.
But really, the Buddha said, there isn't any self in it.
There's just these five kinds of experience.

Maybe it strikes you that there isn't a category of experience called thought in the five categories, which may seem strange because, as we know, thought is such an important element of human experience.
The reason that thought doesn't appear as one of the categories is that the Buddha conceived of thought as a species of perception.
But he realized, of course, that there is a difference between thinking of thought and seeing a tree.
And yet, the two things are actually quite similar.
You see a tree with your eye, but of course, that's not enough.
If there was just an eye sitting there on a table, it's not going to see a tree, right?
It needs to be connected to a brain and consciousness.
You see a tree with eye and eye consciousness; that's visual consciousness.
And you think of thought with your mind and mind consciousness.
So the Buddha conceived of the mind as a kind of species of sense organ, somewhat different from an eye or an ear, just as an ear is pretty different from an eye.
Seeing something and hearing something are radically different kinds of experiences, although we round it off and we say, oh, I see the bird, listen to the bird.
I think it's one thing, but actually it's totally different.
And the mind is different as well.

But the Buddha conceived of it as a sense organ and thought as a non-material object of the sense organ mind, just like a tree actually is also a non-material experience in the mind, based on a physical object, a tree.
So the Buddha considered thinking a species of perception, a kind of perception.
And I have always appreciated the genius of this.
It is so counterintuitive to the way we would see it.
It's really revolutionary and it is very relevant to our practice.
In our world, we just assume that thinking is a whole different thing from seeing and hearing, categorically different.
This is one of the deepest thoughts of our Western tradition.
Thinking is the boss.
The mind is the boss.
The body is just like a little stand for carrying the mind around.
Thinking is associated with mind, which is associated with spirit.
And spirit and mind are the boss.
They can lord it over this merely material world.
So right away, we have suffering right there, right?
Because now we're in exile.
Right away we're in exile: body from mind, us from earth.
So the Buddha saw that right away our conception of thinking was going to produce a lot of suffering.
Because when the mind is in exile from the body, from the physical world, this is pain.
There's no home.
The mind is wandering endlessly in the desert of its utter loneliness.
So the Buddha saw that mind and body have to be united in one experience.
And that's one really good working definition of sitting practice.
We're sitting, unifying body and mind.
Which we're literally doing, right?
Literally we're doing that.
We don't do it very well, but the effort is to take the mind that's swirling all over the place and bring it into union with the body.
Pay attention to the body when you're sitting.
Pay attention to the breathing when you're sitting.
Unify body and mind.
Ground it.
Bring the mind home.
And as I say, however imperfectly we will do this, this is a powerful thing.
There's already a lot of sanity just in however much we can unify body and mind.
Just that alone.
Unifying body and mind.
Unifying body and earth.
Because body is earth, right?
It's the same stuff.
Literally the same stuff.
Unifying body and mind already, we're healing ourselves.
So this was a fantastic discovery of the Buddha.
If the Buddha just stopped there, we would give him a lot of credit.
Thinking is not ours.
Like we've been saying, thinking is not us.
Like a tree that appears in front of our eyes because of conditions in the world, nobody blames themselves for seeing a tree.
Oh damn, why is there a tree?
Why did I have to see this?
Nobody does that.
It's ridiculous, you know?
But yet we blame ourselves that a thought appears in the mind.
But it's the same.
Just like a tree that appears in front of our eyes because of conditions in the world, a thought appears in our mind exactly the same way, because of conditions in the world.
Thoughts are not our fault.
They don't belong to us.
They don't define us.
They are natural phenomena.
And when we ground our thoughts in body and in presence, we can find some liberation in them, even if they're kind of nasty rotten thoughts.
Also, you may have noticed, there is no mention in the five categories of memory either.
Did you notice that?
Again, the Buddha felt that the usual conception of memory already immediately constellates itself.
Just in the idea of memory, as we usually think of it, there's already some suffering.
This happened to me some time ago.
This is me.
This is my story.
This is my experience.
And this explains why I am such a mess today.
Also, besides that, the idea of memory implies a whole host of absolutely unfounded assumptions about time, doesn't it?
So when we think we're having a memory and we hold it in the usual way, the conditions for suffering are already in play.
So the Buddha contrived a way also to understand memory in a different way.
But that's another story.

The important point I'm trying to make now, and hoping not to go on forever, is just that there are five categories, five groups, five heaps, five skandhas, right: form, feeling, perceptions, impulses, consciousness.
Somebody might say, well, actually there's six, there's ten, maybe.
But the Buddha said five.
So we'll just stay with that for now.
Maybe we could improve on it.
I don't know.
When we think of these five as myself, that's when we're in trouble.
When we experience the five as they are, there's no trouble in that.
So here's an early sutta about this, where the Buddha is talking.
This is right after his awakening, where he's talking to the five ascetics who abandoned him when he abandoned asceticism.
They got disgusted with him and then they ran into him later on the road and they were talking.
And the Buddha says this to them.
*The body is not self.
If it were self, it wouldn't get sick.* You could tell the body, "Don't get sick.
I don't like that.
Be like this."
Well, all the time.
*But because the body is not the self, it does get sick.
And you can't say to the body, be this way, not that way.
Feelings are not the self.
If they were the self, they wouldn't torment you the way they do.
You could just tell your feelings*, and we try this all the time, right?
*Be like this, don't be like that.* But it doesn't work, right?
They're going to be the way they are because they're not ourselves.
They don't listen to us.
They do torment us.
You can't tell them, "Be like this and don't be like that."
*Perceptions are not self.
If they were self, they wouldn't trouble you.
You could tell your perceptions, be like that, don't be like this.
But because they're not you, they do trouble you.* And you do have to perceive things you don't like all the time.
*Because you can't tell them, be like this, don't be like that.
Inclinations or volitions, impulses are not the self.
If they were, they would not distress you.
You could tell your impulses, be like this, don't be like that.
Because they're not you, they persist in distressing you.
And you can't tell them, be the way I want you to be.
Consciousness is not self.
If it were, it wouldn't disturb you.
You could tell your consciousness, be like this and don't be like that.
But because it's not the self, it does disturb you.
You can't tell it, be like this, don't be like that.*
*So, what do you think?* He addresses them.
*Are body, feelings, perceptions, inclinations and consciousness permanent or impermanent?* And they say, of course, impermanent.
We've noticed.
And then he said to them, *so is something that's impermanent going to make you happy?
Or is it going to make you suffer?* And they said, more or less, it's going to make you suffer.
Elsewhere, the Buddha acknowledges that, yes, impermanent things can make you temporarily happy, but eventually suffer.
If they didn't also make you temporarily happy, they wouldn't be so problematic.
Right?
We can delude ourselves into thinking we'll get more of the good stuff and not too much of the bad stuff.
But no, ultimately, the impermanent is not good, it's suffering.
*Then he says, is it right to think of something impermanent and fickle that is going to give rise to suffering as, this is mine, I am this, this is myself?* And they say, no, it doesn't make sense.

*He says, therefore, whether it be a past, present, or future body, one's own body or somebody else's body, a gross body or a subtle body, an inferior or superior body, a distant or close body, each body should be seen with true intelligence as it really is.
This isn't mine.
I'm not this.
This is not myself.
And so it is with any feeling, perception, inclination, or consciousness.
Each should be seen with true intelligence as it really is.
This is not mine.
I'm not this.
This isn't myself.*
Seeing things this way, the Buddha goes on: *The attentive, noble disciple disengages from the body, feelings, perceptions, inclinations, and consciousness.
Disengaging, she becomes dispassionate.
Through dispassion, she is freed.
She knows, I'm free.
She understands, birth is overcome and the good life has been lived.
What needs to be done has been done.
There'll be no more of this pain again.* And that's what the Buddha said.

And the five ascetics were so inspired by these words that while the discourse was being spoken, through non-clinging, the minds of the group of five were freed from influences and they became awakened.
And now there were six arhats in the world instead of just one.
The Buddha was the first one and now all these five immediately became arhats, a happy ending.
So this happens with great frequency in the early sutras.
The Buddha says a bunch of stuff and all of a sudden people become enlightened.
Would that it were so, right?
Just hear a bunch of stuff and then boom.
So the Buddha must have had a great charisma.
Or maybe not.
Maybe that was just a way of expressing the wonderful teaching, the appreciation for how wonderful the teaching is.

Maybe if we were writing a story in our days, of an objective person who had a memoir, we would say something like, "And when the Buddha said this, I totally understood it and I was never the same again."
Which is the same thing.
Which happens, right?
Such things do happen.

Even in our times when we don't have the presence of the Buddha anymore, we can hear something like we're hearing something this week, not just theoretically as an idea, but hearing it with our whole body and our whole heart.
And when we do hear it, little by little, we are not the same again, as many here can attest.
Our lives are different.
Our basic, deeply held underlying attitudes soften up and we begin to become a different person.
Probably, I'm guessing, when you heard the language in the sutta of disengagement and dispassion, you were underwhelmed by the idea of disengagement and dispassion.
But I'm reminding you that just a few days ago we were quoting Shantideva, who spoke about pride, "I will do this."
He spoke about passion, even addictive passion, remember, for the good.
Which sounds like almost the opposite of this.
And it is the opposite.
So there are lots of ways of seeing this and lots of ways of talking about it, some of which we like more than others.
And the Buddha didn't really care to get just the right, true thing to say.
This was not his concern.
He understood that everything is misunderstood anyway.
What kind of truth are we going to be able to express?
So he was just concerned that somehow he could find a way to help us think about our lives so that we could let go of our usual obsessions and not have so much suffering.
Famously they say the Buddha taught no self or non-self.
But this is not quite true.
The teachings are definitely not encouraging us to somehow not have a self or think that we don't have a self, or if we do have a self there's something wrong with us.
We should somehow be selfless.
The teachings are not saying that.
They're encouraging us to hold our self with a minimum of pain and a maximum of love and see the truth about our self, that it isn't ours and it isn't us, and that we are who we are for a reason.
So here's another early sutta, a short one, that makes this point.
This is some monastic called Vacchagotta.
He says to the Buddha, "So, Master Gautama, is there a self?"
The Buddha says nothing.
"So then, Master Gautama, is there no self?"
The Buddha says nothing.
And Vacchagotta, I guess, in disgust, left.
I wanted an answer, you know.
No answer.
After Vacchagotta left, the Buddha said to Ananda, "Well, if I had said there is no self, then I would have been siding with the nihilists.
And if I had said, yes, there is a self, then I would have been siding with the eternalists."
In other words, self, no self, these are extreme views, exaggerations.
So to clear this point up, I thought I would bring in another Zen story, because as we know, the Zen tradition is always good for clarifying everything.
So this is 251 in Dogen's collection of 300 stories.
And this is about our friends, the Dharma brothers, Da Wu and Yun Yang, that we always read about.
They're the protagonists of some of our most favorite Zen stories.
And in this particular story, not so well known, Yun Yang is sick, possibly gravely ill, possibly on his deathbed.

And Da Wu says to him, *"Apart from this leaky boat, where will we meet?"* And Yun Yang answers, *"We meet at the place of no birth and death."* And Da Wu said, *"Why not say we won't meet at the place that is not no birth and death?"*
So I said a minute ago, we are who we are for a reason.
And this is the point.
We are who we are not to isolate us and make us suffer.
That's not why we are ourselves.
We are ourselves because it provides a way for us to meet one another, to really meet in loving kindness, beyond what an ordinary, limited, self-centered self is capable of.
And we all already know this.
You don't have to do sesshin to know this.
Everybody knows this.
Everybody knows love is great.
You don't find that many people who are anti-love: "I'm against it.
I don't believe in it.
I think it's a bad idea."
I mean, you can find somebody, I'm sure, but a small minority of people.
Everybody believes that love is a great thing.
And we're all yearning for love because love is liberation.
Love is liberation from the prison of our aloneness.
And everybody understands this and everybody is looking for love.
But mostly we can't really do it because we're too mesmerized by the spell of ourself.
But every now and then, somehow or other, people who don't even do sesshin manage to feel a moment of love.
How do they do that without doing sesshin?
It's impossible, but somehow they do it.
A moment in which we surpass ourselves and we are freed from ourselves.
And if we didn't have ourself, we wouldn't be able to have those moments of transcending ourselves.
We wouldn't be able to love.
And this is why it is so important to clarify the self, to really understand the nature of the self.
So in the story, we know Da Wu from other stories.
He's a pretty crusty and unsentimental Zen guy.
And he's saying to his dear brother Yunyan, if you die right now, where are we going to meet again?
Maybe he's even suppressing a tear when he says this.
And Yunyan says, in effect, don't worry, brother.
Our meeting, as it has been, is already beyond birth and death.
It's already beyond me and you.
It's been a perfect, a complete meeting.
I'm confident in our connection to one another.
And even death won't end it.
But of course Da Wu is so funny.
He will never, ever let Yunyan have the last word.
Yunyan could be dying and Da Wu will insist on correcting him.
So he says, why not say we won't meet where there isn't no birth and death.
So here I think is a beautiful expression of the beautiful, crazy and wonderful paradox of love.
When we really and truly meet one another, it's beyond meeting.
Meeting is always some sort of negotiation.
This is beyond that.
When we really meet each other, it's beyond negotiation.
When self surrenders itself in love, there's no meeting.
Because there aren't two people anymore.
The deepest meeting, in other words, is beyond meeting.
And this is why when we practice together, we become so close.
I think it's why I said in the beginning, whenever I come to Samish, I feel like I've never left.
I've always been here.
Because love kind of disintegrates time.
We get so close practicing together.
And yet at the same time, we hardly know each other at all.
We don't even know each other.
It's weird.
In love, lovers disappear.
And the only thing left is a sense of deep belonging.
And yet, in the middle of that belonging, every one of us is completely alone and all inclusive of everything else.
It's weird.
So I was quoting Shantideva, Bodhisattva Charyavatara.
And it ends with a long and famously complicated chapter about emptiness, which we were talking about yesterday.
He has a really long chapter about emptiness, which is hard to penetrate.
But in the chapter, there's one little verse where there's a skeptic.
Like a skeptic is raising objections, and the emptiness sage is answering objections.
So the skeptic says, well, if self is empty, and there really isn't any self, who are we going to have compassion for?
It's a good question.
And here's the way the sage answers.
This is usually paraphrased, but I'm going to give you the exact quotation from the translation by our wise and skillful translators.
This is what it says.
*Who do we have compassion for?
For anyone projected through the delusion, which is embraced for the sake of what has to be done.*
Is that great?
*Who do we have compassion for?
For anyone projected through the delusion, which is embraced for the sake of what has to be done.*
And this is so great.
We are not trying to overcome delusion and get it right.
This is not our effort in practice.
We come to recognize that we, ourself, are delusion embodied.
We are.
And we appreciate this.
We know it.
We're not fooled by it.
And we think it's great.
And we embrace it.
As Shantideva says, we embrace the delusion of self for the sake of what has to be done, compassion.
And this is how we can weep over the sad world and work tirelessly, as hard as we can, to try to help things, even though we know it's all right.
It's okay.
Very short story.
Hui Chao asked Fayan, "What is Buddha?"
Fayan said, "You are Hui Chao."
The name Hui Chao.
And we all have names.
We have names that we were given by our parents, names that we receive in the practice.
Every name means something and implies a destiny.
The name Hui Chao means going beyond wisdom.
And this is more or less what Shantideva is saying to us in his verse.
We go beyond wisdom back into delusion for the sake of what has to be done.
And also because we understand that there is no other way.
Buddha is going beyond Buddha.
That's what Dogen says again and again and again.
We have to go beyond Buddha.
Fully be ourselves.
Go beyond Buddha.
Hui Chao is only Hui Chao.
You are only you.
I am only me.
That's great.
For all of our suffering, it's amazing.
And we embrace the delusion of self.
We appreciate it.
We understand it as it really is.
And we hold it with quiet appreciation, even in all of its pain and confusion.
Because this is the way we meet one another, and not meet one another, always with as much love and understanding as we possibly can muster today.
And there's always more.
Always more.
So the kind of effort that we make in our sitting is to just show up and investigate what's here now, without thinking it's supposed to be this way, it's supposed to be that way.
It's always supposed to be exactly the way it is.
And we embrace the delusion of this moment.
And we meet ourselves.
And we meet one another, moment after moment.
So thank you.
And welcome to the new folks.
A couple new folks came, I guess.
I see some faces that I know that weren't here before.
Although who knows if they were actually confused.
Who is here or is here now, I don't even know.
But if you are just arriving, welcome.
Thanks for coming.

verbatim.text: We were talking yesterday, saying that the Buddha wasn't so much concerned about the truth, or the nature of the universe, or how things came to be. He was mostly concerned about suffering, and we all know the story about the Buddha having encountered suffering, left home, and went on his spiritual quest up until that super dramatic moment under the Bodhi tree. Everybody knows that story. And every year in Mexico, during our annual Rohatsu sesshin, I gin myself up to tell this story with full elaboration. We all get really excited about the Buddha's awakening. And then we end our session with a really colorful and musical, flower-strewn, outrageous ceremony to celebrate our collective enlightenment. And it is really great. Some of you have been there, I know.

And you can ask Rick and Arhelia, who have been there many times. And they will tell you that it is probably the greatest, most joyful enlightenment ceremony on earth. It is, I think. Modestly, I'm saying this. I don't think you'll find a ceremony like this anywhere on earth. So yes, the Buddha's awakening is a very dramatic, joyful, wonderful thing, as we read about it in the Sutras.
